10.0.0.en: Shamir: it lies between Hanin and Samaria.

10.0.1.en: Mount Ephraim: mountainous lands lying in the portion of the tribe of Ephraim (map 12). Abimelech died, and, as we mentioned, he is not counted among the judges because he seized the kingship out of love of rulership; and after that God raised up a judge to rule by His law, "Tola." He was of the tribe of Issachar but dwelt in Ephraim, and peace prevailed in his days, and the people lived by God's commandments, and the enemies did not attack the children of Israel.

10.1.0.en: After Tola had fulfilled his task as deliverer and judge of his people for twenty-three years, he died and was buried in his city.

10.1.1.en: If you are in a position of responsibility in your home, in the Church or in any place, follow God's commandments and teach by them, and you will strengthen the faith of those around you and give them the divine peace, so that they live in faith in God's hands.

10.2.0.en: After "Tola" another judge arose to judge, "Jair," who was called the Gileadite because he dwelt in the land of Gilead east of the Jordan. The length of his judging the people was 22 years, during which nothing happened to disturb the calm and security that prevailed throughout the period of his rule. He taught the people God's law and judged by it to settle the disputes and problems among them. It appears that peace prevailed in his time, for no wars are mentioned throughout the length of his judgeship.

10.3.0.en: Havoth-jair: that is, the farms of Jair, lying in the northwestern part of Bashan, east of the Jordan.

10.3.1.en: The land of Gilead: the region east of the Jordan inhabited by the clan of the Gileadites, named after their head, who was the son of Machir and the grandson of Manasseh.

10.3.2.en: Camon: a place in the land of Gilead (map 12). The ancients married at an early age and rejoiced in an abundance of offspring, and Jair had a number of wives, by whom he begat thirty sons, each of whom had an ass, as the notables of the people did in that age, and they had thirty farms in the land of Gilead, with buildings and installations, which were therefore considered cities; and they were called "the farms of Jair," and the names of those cities were preserved as they were until the time the book was written.

10.4.0.en: After Jair had judged his people, he died and was buried in one of the cities of Gilead, which was called "Camon."

10.4.1.en: Hold fast to God's commandments so as to apply them in your life, and then you will be able to teach them to others, and they will be what governs your works and with which you guide others, and you will live in tranquility and peace.

10.5.s.en: (3) The Philistines and the children of Ammon humble Israel

10.5.0.en: Ashtaroth: plural of Ashtar, who is the goddess of the moon.

10.5.1.en: Aram: lies northeast of Canaan; it is the land of present-day Syria, and its capital is Damascus.

10.5.2.en: Zidon: it is Sidon, lying on the Mediterranean south of Tyre.

10.5.3.en: Moab: they dwell east of the Jordan and the Dead Sea.

10.5.4.en: The children of Ammon: they dwell east of the Jordan and north of Moab.

10.5.5.en: The Philistines: they dwelt in the south of the land of Canaan, from the Dead Sea to the Mediterranean.

10.5.6.en: As has often been repeated in the Book of Judges, the people had rested for a period of time from the harassment of the enemies, and then repeated the same transgression they had committed before, which had been the cause of the Lord's leaving them to fall into the hands of their enemies. Here they are, after the death of Jair the Gileadite, grieving the Lord anew, for they began to worship the gods of the pagan nations surrounding them.

10.6.0.en: Since they forsook the Lord, He too forsook them, and in His anger against them He withdrew His protection and left them as spoil in the hand of their enemies who surrounded them, the Philistines from the west and the children of Ammon from the east, so they fell under their grip and became slaves to them.

10.7.0.en: "They vexed and oppressed the children of Israel": that is, they struck them with blows that left clear marks on their bodies and crushed them; the meaning is that they humbled them greatly by beating and exploitation.

10.7.1.en: The people tasted the bitterness of slavery anew as the fruit of their evil; since they despised the Lord and forsook His worship, their enemies humbled them and they remained in humiliation for 18 years, and they were greatly distressed. Those who suffered the most harm by reason of their location were the tribes of Reuben and Gad and the eastern half-tribe of Manasseh, the tribes that dwelt east of the Jordan on the lands that had belonged to the Amorites before the children of Israel took them from them, among which are also the mountains of Gilead.

10.8.0.en: The weariness and humiliation were not confined to the eastern tribes alone, but the Ammonites crossed the Jordan to fight the tribes dwelling in the west, among them the tribes of Judah, Benjamin and Ephraim, which are the largest tribes of Israel, to bring them under their control, which plunged Israel into severe distress.

10.8.1.en: If you neglect your relationship with God, you will lose His care and protection, and consequently the devil will gain dominion over you through many sins and will humble you, because he is fierce and wants your destruction. So return quickly, for God your Father is merciful, and He will forgive you and embrace you and save you from the humiliation of Satan.

10.9.0.en: From the distress of slavery the children of Israel cried out to God to save them, as this was repeated several times in the age of the judges, and they confessed their sin, that they had worshiped the pagan gods and forsaken God.

10.10.0.en: God reminded them, by the tongue of the high priest or one of the prophets, how He had saved them when they cried to Him to rescue them from the slavery of the surrounding nations who humbled them, such as His delivering them from the Egyptians: He brought them out of their slavery by the hand of Moses.

10.10.1.en: And from the Amorites: He gave them victory over their kings and gave them their land (Num 21:21-35, Josh 11:3). And from the children of Ammon: He prepared His servant Ehud, who killed Eglon their king (ch. 3:12-30). And from the Philistines there was Shamgar, who killed 600 men of them with an ox goad (ch. 3:3, 21). And from the Zidonians the Lord delivered His people by the hand of Barak and Deborah (ch. 5:19). And from the Amalekites the Lord delivered them, whether in the days of Moses by the hand of Joshua (Ex 17) or by the hand of Gideon (ch. 6:3). And from the Maonites the Lord delivered His people by the hand of Ehud and Gideon (chs. 3, 6). The Maonites are the inhabitants of Maon, which lies in the land of Edom east of the Jordan.

10.11.0.en: But the people, in return for these kindnesses of God, betrayed His covenants and forsook His worship and departed from Him and went after other, false gods; therefore He will not save them, since they have denied Him and become strangers to Him. Why then do they cry to Him now? So God says to them: Go to those whom you have chosen as your gods, that perhaps they may save you from your distress. This is a style of reproach, by which God mocks them, because the pagan gods are unable to save them.

10.12.0.en: The people confess their fault and place themselves in God's hands, to punish them or to pardon them as He wills, but they entreat Him repentantly to rescue them from the enemy and then to discipline them if He wishes.

10.13.0.en: "His soul was grieved for the misery of Israel": God condescends and expresses His feeling in emotions that human beings understand, namely His being distressed because of their humiliation, and this shows His tenderness and fatherhood; for if He threatens His people, it is that they may repent and He may have mercy on them.

10.13.1.en: The repentance of the people was a practical repentance, for they broke the idols and tore down their altars and returned to obedience to their heavenly Father and to His worship, and the Lord's heart was softened because of the hardship to which His people were exposed.

10.13.2.en: Confession of the fault alone is not enough to obtain forgiveness, but it must be accompanied by an act that shows regret and repentance, and the removal of every cause of the sin into which a person had fallen, the correction of bad conduct, and a sincere resolve not to repeat it; and what confirms the soundness of his resolve is that good works take the place of the corrupt works he had committed before. Let us then be earnest in our repentance by offering good works that please the Lord.

10.14.s.en: (5) The children of Ammon prepare to fight Israel

10.14.0.en: Mizpah: it lies in the portion of the tribe of Gad and was called Mizpah of Gilead (ch. 11:29) and Ramath-mizpeh (Josh 13:26); it is the place of the heap which Jacob and the people of Laban set up as a witness to the covenant between them (Gen 31:49). The children of Ammon gathered their armies to fight the children of Israel, beginning with the tribes dwelling in Gilead. And the children of Israel prepared with their armies to defend themselves and encamped in one of the places of Gilead called "Mizpah."

10.15.0.en: The children of Israel were taking counsel among themselves as to who should be the leader to lead them in this war of theirs, and this brave person would be worthy of their swearing allegiance to him as head and ruler over them in all their lands east of the Jordan.

10.15.1.en: Do not be disturbed by the snares of the devil and his wars, for your God is stronger than he and is able to give you victory over him; but be watchful and hold fast to your spiritual striving, and you will certainly win.

10.15.2.en: The victory over the children of Ammon

11.0.s.en: (1) The choice of Jephthah as head over Gilead

11.0.0.en: In this chapter the inspired writer begins by narrating the Lord's intervening anew to rescue His people in response to their prayers, their repentance and their supplications. From this verse onward he makes known to us the person of the new judge whom the Lord chose to save His people by him, "Jephthah," surnamed the Gileadite, after his father Gilead and his homeland, the land of Gilead.

11.0.1.en: Gilead's wife bore no sons, so Gilead sinned with a harlot woman, and she bore him Jephthah. Here appears the mercy of God, who does not punish a man for the evil of his father so long as he walks with God and holds fast to His commandments, but rather chooses him as a leader of his people.

11.1.0.en: But after the birth of Jephthah his lawful wife bore sons, and when they grew up they drove Jephthah out from among them, saying to him that he was the son of a harlot woman and had no right to inherit with them.

11.2.0.en: After Jephthah was driven out from his brothers, he dwelt in the land of Tob on the border of Gilead, and idle men gathered around him who had no means of livelihood except plundering the money of travelers on the traveled roads and working as mercenaries for whoever paid the price, and Jephthah accompanied them and led them in their adventures.

11.3.0.en: The children of Ammon began to fight the children of Israel in order to enslave and humble them.

11.4.0.en: The elders of Gilead were exchanging views and counsel as to who could lead their armies to face the Ammonites. The opinion settled on Jephthah because of his bravery and strength, so they went to him and asked him to lead them in the war against the children of Ammon.

11.5.0.en: Jephthah reminded them of their bad conduct toward him when they agreed with his brothers to drive him out from among them, and he marveled at their new behavior toward him, for how, after they had driven him out of his father's house, could they come and ask him to help them when they were exposed to the harassment of enemies?

11.5.1.en: And Jephthah, whom his brothers drove out and then returned asking for his leadership to save them, is a symbol of Christ, whom His people rejected and crucified, and then returned asking for salvation at His hands when they believed in Him.

11.6.0.en: "Be our head": be a ruler over us and a leader to us.

11.6.1.en: The content of the elders' reply carried a tone of apology for what had gone before on their part, and that they were coming to him now to set right what had passed, and here they ask him to be head over all the inhabitants of Gilead.

11.7.0.en: Jephthah made it a condition for the children of Israel that if they brought him back to his country to fight the children of Ammon, and if God gave him victory in his war against them and delivered them into his hand, he would become head over them. Jephthah set this condition to confirm the agreement, lest they return to their former way with him and deny him after the victory.

11.8.0.en: The elders assured him of their readiness to set him up as head, and called the Lord to witness to their covenant with him.

11.9.0.en: "Jephthah uttered all his words before the LORD": he prayed to the Lord and pledged before Him to act.

11.9.1.en: Mizpah: a city in Gilead east of the Jordan River, at which Jacob made a covenant with Laban. There are five other cities named Mizpah in other places.

11.9.2.en: Jephthah went with them, and the people appointed him head over them and commander of their armies. Then he set out for the war with a deep prayer in the place where they had gathered to set him up as head, "Mizpah," and in this prayer of his is a confession that God is the One able to give him victory, and he asks Him to be with him.

11.9.3.en: How beautiful it is to begin every new work with prayer to the Lord, asking His help and the accomplishment of His good will. If the work agrees with His good will, may He guide us to the right way to complete it with all sincerity and faithfulness, and if it is harmful to us, may He keep us away from it.

11.9.4.en: (2) Jephthah's correspondence with the kings of the Ammonites, Edom, Moab and the king of the Amorites (vv. 12-28:) 12 And Jephthah sent messengers unto the king of the children of Ammon, saying, What hast thou to do with me, that thou art come against me to fight in my land? 13 And the king of the children of Ammon answered unto the messengers of Jephthah, Because Israel took away my land, when they came up out of Egypt, from Arnon even unto Jabbok, and unto Jordan: now therefore restore those lands again peaceably. 14 And Jephthah sent messengers again unto the king of the children of Ammon: 15 And said unto him, Thus saith Jephthah, Israel took not away the land of Moab, nor the land of the children of Ammon: 16 But when Israel came up from Egypt, and walked through the wilderness unto the Red sea, and came to Kadesh; 17 Then Israel sent messengers unto the king of Edom, saying, Let me, I pray thee, pass through thy land: but the king of Edom would not hearken thereto. And in like manner they sent unto the king of Moab: but he would not consent: and Israel abode in Kadesh. 18 Then they went along through the wilderness, and compassed the land of Edom, and the land of Moab, and came by the east side of the land of Moab, and pitched on the other side of Arnon, but came not within the border of Moab: for Arnon was the border of Moab. 19 And Israel sent messengers unto Sihon king of the Amorites, the king of Heshbon; and Israel said unto him, Let us pass, we pray thee, through thy land into my place. 20 But Sihon trusted not Israel to pass through his coast: but Sihon gathered all his people together, and pitched in Jahaz, and fought against Israel. 21 And the LORD God of Israel delivered Sihon and all his people into the hand of Israel, and they smote them: so Israel possessed all the land of the Amorites, the inhabitants of that country. 22 And they possessed all the coasts of the Amorites, from Arnon even unto Jabbok, and from the wilderness even unto Jordan. 23 So now the LORD God of Israel hath dispossessed the Amorites from before his people Israel, and shouldest thou possess it? 24 Wilt not thou possess that which Chemosh thy god giveth thee to possess? So whomsoever the LORD our God shall drive out from before us, them will we possess. 25 And now art thou any thing better than Balak the son of Zippor, king of Moab? did he ever strive against Israel, or did he ever fight against them, 26 While Israel dwelt in Heshbon and her towns, and in Aroer and her towns, and in all the cities that be along by the coasts of Arnon, three hundred years? why therefore did ye not recover them within that time? 27 Wherefore I have not sinned against thee, but thou doest me wrong to war against me: the LORD the Judge be judge this day between the children of Israel and the children of Ammon. 28 Howbeit the king of the children of Ammon hearkened not unto the words of Jephthah which he sent him.

11.10.0.en: This verse and the following verses relate the content of the two messages of Jephthah which he sent to the king of Ammon, asking for peace and explaining his right to the land over which the king of the children of Ammon was disputing with him. The king of the children of Ammon replied to his first message but did not reply to his second message. The content of his first message was his asking what had happened that the king of the children of Ammon had come intending war against the children of Israel.

11.11.0.en: The reply of the king of the children of Ammon to Jephthah's messengers contained a historical fallacy, for he accused Israel of seizing what he claimed had been his own land, the region lying between the two tributaries of the Jordan east of the river, namely Arnon and Jabbok (Num 21:13, 21-30). These lands the children of Israel had taken from the king of the Amorites, not from the king of the children of Ammon as he claimed. The king of the Amorites had taken them earlier from the children of Ammon and Moab, so Israel took nothing of these lands from the hand of the children of Ammon.

11.12.0.en: On the basis of the reply of the king of the children of Ammon, Jephthah sent him what refutes this claim of his, in a lengthy account of the true history of the possession of these lands.

11.13.0.en: He showed him historical facts proving that the children of Israel had not taken any of the lands of the children of Ammon, nor even of the children of Moab, the cousins of the children of Ammon.

11.14.0.en: "Came up": because the land of Palestine is higher than the land of Egypt.

11.14.1.en: Jephthah relates that the children of Israel, when they came out of Egypt, walked in the desert lying east of the barren Delta and crossed the Red Sea, and from it to Kadesh (Num 20:1).

11.15.0.en: "The king of Edom would not hearken": he did not respond to their request.

11.15.1.en: "He would not consent": he did not agree.

11.15.2.en: From Kadesh Israel sent messengers to the king of Edom, asking permission merely to pass through his land, but the king of Edom refused and threatened to wage war on Israel if it dared to enter his land, and the same story happened with the king of Moab. So they were forced to remain for a short time in Kadesh to replan their journey toward the Promised Land, after the roads through the land of Edom and the land of Moab had been closed to them (Num 20:14-18).

11.16.0.en: "Compassed the land of Edom and the land of Moab": the children of Israel went around the land of Edom and the land of Moab in a barren desert to avoid passing through the land of Edom and Moab when they refused that.

11.16.1.en: "Arnon was the border of Moab": the boundary of the land of Moab is one of the tributaries of the Jordan, called Arnon, which separates Moab from the Amorites.

11.16.2.en: In their journey the people avoided the land of Moab and the children of Ammon so as not to stir up a war against them, and made a hard journey going around the land of Edom and the land of Moab, then came from the east side to reach, from outside the borders of the land of Moab, the other bank of the river Arnon, being careful in this not to touch the lands of Moab.

11.17.0.en: Heshbon: it lies between the rivers Jabbok and Arnon (map 11). From there the children of Israel sent messengers to the king of the Amorites, asking him to allow them to pass through his land so as to reach the land which the Lord had promised the children of Israel, but the king of the Amorites did not permit him either (Num 21:21-30).

11.18.0.en: Jahaz: a Moabite city (map 11). The king of the Amorites was fearful of the request of the children of Israel and suspected deceit on their part, for perhaps their purpose was not only passing through but occupying his land, so he hastened and formed an army and rushed to fight the children of Israel at the town of "Jahaz" (Num 21:23).

11.18.1.en: Jephthah was patient in his dealing with the king of the children of Ammon, despite the latter's false claims and his evil intention toward the children of Israel. This is a good example for us to try to take every possible way of achieving peace between us and others, acting on the saying of the Gospel, "If it be possible, as much as lieth in you, live peaceably with all men."

11.19.0.en: The Lord delivered the Amorites into the hand of the children of Israel, and they possessed the lands which the king of the Ammonites now claims without right.

11.20.0.en: By their victory over the Amorites the children of Israel took all the lands of the Amorites lying between the river Arnon in the south and the river Jabbok in the north, and from the desert in the east to the river Jordan in the west.

11.21.0.en: Jephthah says in this message of his to the king of the children of Ammon that the Lord had supported the children of Israel and given them victory over the Amorites, and thus it is God who granted them those lands to dwell in, so how do you think of taking them from them by your false claims?

11.22.0.en: Jephthah continued his words to the king of the children of Ammon, saying to him that it is his right to take possession only of the lands that his god "Chemosh" enables him to have, while they have the right to take possession of the lands that God Jehovah enables them to have. By this Jephthah mocks the pagan god Chemosh, whom the children of Ammon worship, who is unable to support his worshipers.

11.23.0.en: Jephthah goes on, saying to him: Are you stronger than Balak king of Moab, who was afraid of the victories that our people had won over the peoples of the region and did not dare to face the children of Israel, so he summoned Balaam the son of Beor to curse Israel so that they would not be able to invade his land (Num 22-24)? And he never thought of fighting them.

11.24.0.en: Heshbon: the capital of the kingdom of Sihon.

11.24.1.en: Aroer: it lies north of the river Arnon (map 10). Three hundred years: the children of Israel took the lands of the Amorites in 1452 B.C., and Jephthah's victory over the children of Ammon was in 1143 B.C., so the period that had passed was about 300 years. "Three hundred years have now passed since our settling in these lands, namely Heshbon and Aroer and the cities of Arnon, since our victory over the Amorites who dwelt in them before us, so where was your people throughout all this time, and none of their kings thought of recovering them as you are trying to do now?"

11.25.0.en: In this Jephthah showed his people's right to the land over which the king of the children of Ammon was disputing with him, and that he had not encroached on any of his lands and had never sinned against him. As for the king of the children of Ammon, by thinking of war against him he had committed a great error, and it is God, who is just and knows the intentions of men, who will judge for all.

11.26.0.en: Despite all these proofs and evidences that Jephthah brought, the king of the children of Ammon did not wish to be persuaded by them, but clung to his mistaken thought and rejected Jephthah's peace overtures and decided to go on with the decision for war.

11.26.1.en: The stand of the king of the children of Ammon after the long defense that Jephthah presented shows the hateful clinging to one's opinion even if it is wrong, which is a vice that may bring its owner to utter destruction, just as happened to the king of the children of Ammon. The man in whom there is not the Spirit of the Lord does not accept the call to the truth, does not listen to the counsel of others, and does not like to heed one who warns him of the danger of his position. So the end of such a man is a ruin to him. May the Lord grant us spiritual senses so that we perceive the advice that others may offer us, and listen, and humble ourselves before our spiritual guides.

11.27.0.en: The Holy Spirit came upon Jephthah, granting him courage and confidence to do what he had been charged with, and guided him to pass through the cities to stir up the people and rouse them to defend their cities and to gather the soldiers who would be his army. The cities through which he passed were Gilead and Mizpah of Gilead.

11.28.0.en: Jephthah vowed a vow to offer to the Lord at his victory in his war against the children of Ammon, namely that the first one who would meet him from his house on his return victorious he would offer up as a burnt offering to the Lord. In this vow Jephthah was influenced by the customs of the pagan peoples, who offered human sacrifices, which God absolutely forbade. This is a great error on Jephthah's part. As for God's asking Abraham to offer Isaac as a sacrifice, it was to test him, and he did not in fact offer him (Gen 22).

11.29.1.en: Jephthah attacked the children of Ammon and the Lord gave him victory over them, and he defeated their armies with a crushing defeat in a wide region that included twenty cities, from Aroer even to Minnith, and extended to "the plain of the vineyards," so the children of Ammon surrendered and submitted to the control of the children of Israel and tasted the humiliation of the defeat which they had wanted to inflict on the people of the Lord.

11.30.0.en: When he returned from the war victorious, he came back to his house at "Mizpah," and then came the tragedy, for he was surprised that the first to come out to meet him was his only daughter. She came out to meet him with her companions with timbrels and dances, as was the custom anciently.

11.31.0.en: "He rent his clothes": as is the custom of the people of the East when something happens that greatly grieves them.

11.31.1.en: "I have opened my mouth unto the LORD": I have vowed a vow and cannot go back from it.

11.31.2.en: When her father saw her, he realized the tragedy into which he had fallen, so he rent his clothes in grief and cried, Alas, my daughter, and was distressed because of the vow he had vowed and could not go back on.

11.32.0.en: "According to that which hath proceeded out of thy mouth": as you pronounced your vow.

11.32.1.en: The girl said to her father that since the Lord had given you victory over your enemies and you have vowed a vow, fulfil your vow to which you pledged yourself.

11.33.0.en: The girl made her father understand that she was ready to carry out the vow, on condition that he give her a respite of two months before carrying it out, which she would spend on the mountains with her companions, bewailing her virginity with them.

11.34.0.en: Her father agreed to her request and permitted her to go with her companions as she asked, so she went to the mountains with her companions.

11.35.0.en: "He did with her according to his vow which he had vowed": he offered her as a sacrifice.

11.35.1.en: The daughter of Jephthah kept her promise and returned after the two months had passed and gave herself up to her father. Her father carried out his vow, and she died a virgin who had not married. And it became a custom for the women of the children of Israel to go to the mountains and remain there four days, during which they lament the daughter of Jephthah.

11.35.2.en: It is to be noted that Jephthah made three errors ...

11.35.3.en: The first is that he vowed his daughter, that is, a human being, and God never accepts this; and the second error is that he completed the wrong vow and carried it out, whereas he should rather have drawn back from it and not completed the first error with a second error .. As for his third error, it is that he did not consult any of the priests responsible for the law, who would have dissuaded him from completing his wrong vow. In the New Testament also, the priest, through the authority of the sacrament of the priesthood, can release a person from his wrong vow.

11.35.4.en: God allowed Gideon to kill his daughter to warn all his children to keep away from haste in decisions, lest they lose what is dearest to them, that is, their children.

11.35.5.en: Be careful when you vow, and vow what you are able to fulfil and what at the same time does not violate God's commandments, and it is better to consult your father of confession; for a vow is a great thing that strengthens your faith, but do not spoil it by your rashness and by vowing things beyond your ability.

11.35.6.en: Ephraim's fighting Jephthah, and the judges Ibzan, Elon and Abdon
